1260.heavy: Heavy syllable = nucleus with a VV sequence (/ae ai ao au ei ou/ undergoing diphthong formation, 'creating the heavy nuclei discussed in §1.3'), counting two moras; light syllables have 'only one mora each'. No underlying codas, no contrastive vowel length.
1260.dflt: All-light roots (both regimes agree): trochees from left root edge, primary on rightmost foot head — 2σ σ́σ, 3σ σ́σσ, 4σ σσσ́σ, 5σ σσσ́σσ (penult if even syllable count, antepenult if odd).
1260.prule: Trochaic feet parsed left-to-right from the left margin of the ROOT (prefixes/proclitics/reduplication excluded; suffixes and enclitics included); first and every second subsequent syllable/mora stressed, final odd unit unfooted; PRIMARY stress = rightmost foot head. Older speakers: moraic trochees (heavy = VV/diphthong nuclei, two moras); younger speakers: syllabic trochees regardless of weight (change in progress).
1260.srule: Secondary stress on every foot head except the rightmost: the first syllable/mora of the root and every second one after it are stressed, the rightmost stressed unit carrying primary stress and the others secondary. 2-3-unit words have one stress; 4-5-unit words secondary on the 1st unit, primary on the 3rd (dìhunáre, pàrahágala, kòkotá-nekyu); 6-7 units secondary on 1st and 3rd. Counted in moras by older speakers (VV heavy), in syllables by younger speakers; domain = root + suffixes/enclitics.
1260.quote: Stress in Kokota is characterised by considerable variation, to the extent that a single speaker may assign stress variably to words with certain syllable structures. This results from changes that are under way in the stress assignment regime. The regular stress assignment regime involves feet parsed from left to right, so stress is counted from the left margin of the root. Stress is trochaic, meaning that the first and every second subsequent syllable/mora is stressed. tn.quote: По аналогии с современными енисейскими языками — кетским и югским — можно предполагать, что в К.я. первый тон реализовался на закрытом, а второй — на открытом вокалическом фонемном базисе: hen (= ²hɛˀn) 'сажень', мн. ч. he:naŋ (= ¹he:naŋ) ... Длительность в К.я. связана во многих случаях с характером слогового тона (первый и третий тон являются долгими, а второй — кратким, отрывистым) ... Но в других случаях, особенно в многосложных словах, где тональные различия нейтрализованы, длительность может рассматриваться как фонологически релевантный признак на уровне гласных фонем
tn.translation: By analogy with the modern Yeniseian languages, Ket and Yugh, one may suppose that in Kott the first tone was realised on a close and the second on an open vocalic phonemic base: hen (= ²hɛˀn) 'fathom', pl. he:naŋ (= ¹he:naŋ) ... Length in Kott is in many cases tied to the character of the syllabic tone (the first [and] third tones are long, the second short and abrupt) ... But in other cases, especially in polysyllabic words, where the tonal distinctions are neutralised, length may be regarded as a phonologically relevant feature at the level of vowel phonemes

1277.prule: Tönjes 1910 ('Die Betonung', pp. 7-11) states dynamic word stress (Ton/Starkton/Hauptton) with a Hauptregel: main stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (monosyllabic stems: on the preceding prefix or concord syllable; disyllabic stems: on the stem syllable, which is the penult; stems of four or more syllables: penult; di- and trisyllabic adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, pronouns: penult). Morphologically conditioned deviation: words with a trisyllabic nominal or verbal stem carry the main stress on the stem(-initial) syllable, i.e. the antepenult (omutaleli, okulengula), as does the pluperfect of disyllabic verbs (okua dengele); a listed set of trisyllabic stems (okuangala, okuehena, okufifina, okulotoka, okunangala) keeps penult stress. The concord syllables ta (present indicative) and na (jussive; negative imperfect/perfect) and the negative particles ha, ke, ka always carry main stress; before an enclitic (xo, xe, mo/po/ko, jo, nge, sa, 'lje, uja, the monosyllabic nominal and verbal stems, and the demonstratives edi, ei) the host word is stressed on its final syllable. The modern description (Halme 2004, known only from the publisher's text; Wikipedia citing it) is of an H/L tone language; whether Halme treats stress was not checked (see tone).
1277.srule: Tönjes 1910: a Nebenton (secondary stress) placed by morphology, not by alternation — on the penult in trisyllabic-stem words (whose main stress is on the stem-initial syllable); on the stem-initial syllable in words with stems of four or more syllables (main stress on the penult; okuhambelela, okufindikila); a weak Nebenton on word-initial pre-tonic o- and on a monosyllabic pre-tonic subject concord; a weak Nebenton on the final syllable in the negative imperfect/perfect (main stress on na); in reduplications the stem syllables are equally stressed. No Nebenton is mentioned for plain disyllabic-stem words.

evidence_works.detail: Procedure (p. 16): four fieldwork periods (Jul/Aug/Dec 2013, Jul 2014) at San José de la Zorra with three native speakers (two women over 60, one man of 40); the same word and sentence questionnaires applied to each ('Se aplicaron los mismos cuestionarios de palabras y oraciones cada uno de estos informantes'); ~1000-word lexicon, verb paradigms for ~40 lexemes and ~350 sentence items recorded on a Tascam DR-100 and analysed in Praat and CSL. Description (pp. 179-183): disyllables with final stress are unsuffixed roots (/i.ˈma/ 'baila', /hem.ˈpeɬ/ 'lengua'); disyllables with non-final stress carry a syllabic suffix (/ˈtsi.to/ 'beben' < /tsi/); monomorphemic tri-/tetrasyllables have penultimate stress ('Estas palabras son monomorfémicas y el acento cae siempre en la penúltima sílaba', p. 181; list (10), p. 182: /ko.ˈra.ta/, /m.ska.ˈʎa.pa/); prefixed polysyllables keep the root's final stress (/m.to.ˈnak/ 'amarras' < /to.ˈnak/). Generalization p. 183 (row quote, confirmed): monomorphemic words stress the last syllable if disyllabic and the penult if longer; affixes never take stress and the root keeps its stress under affixation. Analysis (sec. 4.3.2, p. 226): a right-aligned asymmetric iambic foot with NO-FIN active only above two syllables, plus the morphological constraint *[AFIJO] 'demanda que los afijos no formen parte del material que se asocia a los pies, es decir, que no reciban acento' (confirmed). Instrumental part (sec. 4.2.4, pp. 185-193): Praat measurements on two female speakers of vowel duration (ms) and F0 (mean of onset/offset in Hz; trajectory class with a 1.5-semitone threshold) for the last two vowels of multisyllabic words, 66 tokens with final stress and 57 with non-final stress. Final-stress words: stressed vowel 157 ms vs pretonic 105 ms, F0 157 vs 148 Hz (Table 1, p. 189). Non-final-stress words: stressed 132 ms vs posttonic 96 ms, but F0 149 Hz on the stressed vs 179 Hz on the final posttonic syllable ('una separación de aproximadamente 30 hertzios', Table 3, p. 191). The author reads this final high flat pitch as a demarcative tonal prominence, not a second stress: the first syllable of four-syllable words 'no parece recibir un acento secundario' (p. 197), 'es un hecho que la lengua no es tonal' (p. 227), and the DEM constraint keeps the duration-based single stress ('preserva la definición de acento', p. 227). So it agrees with the entry's single root stress with unstressed affixes and with sec_status 'none', and adds a within-root position rule and acoustic correlates for a sister variety.
